Mishima Yukio. A prolific and controversial post-war novelist, playwright, and essayist who fused classical Japanese aesthetics, particularly the samurai code and ritual, with contemporary psychological darkness. His dazzling, baroque prose and obsessive thematic engagement with beauty, death, and masculine honour made him a towering and divisive literary figure until his theatrical suicide by seppuku shocked the world.

His most ambitious work is the tetralogy The Sea of Fertility, completed in 1969 and 1970, spanning Japanese history from the Taisho era through the post-war period and exploring reincarnation, beauty, decay, and the difficulty of maintaining aesthetic purity in a modernized society. The first volume, Spring Snow, is a tragic love story between a young nobleman and a noblewoman set in 1912, suffused with melancholic beauty and the conflict between duty and desire. Beyond novels, Mishima authored numerous plays, including Madame de Sade and modern adaptations of classical Nō theatre, synthesizing experimental form with traditional Japanese dramatic language.

His early work The Sound of Waves, published in 1954, is a romantic idyll set in a fishing village. Yet his later work grows darker, increasingly preoccupied with violence, homosexuality, militarism, and existential nihilism. Mishima practiced martial arts intensively, bodybuilding, and swordplay, fusing physical discipline with literary craft and publicly embodying his values of masculine rigour and traditional Japanese virtue. In 1970, he committed suicide by seppuku, ritual disembowelment, after leading an attempted military coup, performing his aesthetic philosophy in his death—an act of ritualistic beauty pursued to its fatal extreme.
